power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: A Taxonomy of Misleading Mental Health Content Online

author.affiliation:
Department of Communication and Media Research
								University of Zurich

text.text: Online mental health communication can mislead without containing demonstrably incorrect claims.
This article introduces a taxonomy of misleading online mental health content, distinguishing between source-, message-, and decoding-level misleadingness.
It provides researchers, clinicians, and online platforms with a framework for identifying potentially harmful mental health content online that veracity-based approaches may overlook.

Mental health content presents a distinctive challenge for misinformation research: it is a domain where scientific consensus is often contested and evolving, which complicates definitions centered on factual accuracy.

Recent scholarship identifies broader forms of misleading mental health communication, including stigmatizing or overgeneralized messages, and personal experiences presented as broadly applicable evidence (Hoffner et al., 2026; Kaňková et al., 2025; Starvaggi et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Recent scholarship identifies broader forms of misleading mental health communication, including stigmatizing or overgeneralized messages, and personal experiences presented as broadly applicable evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hoffner et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kaňková et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Starvaggi et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A statement such as "I healed without therapy" (No-Alarm9339, 2024) is not misinforming on its face; it becomes misleading when the speaker implies, or readers infer, that therapy is unnecessary (Hall, 1980).
text.formatted: A statement such as "I healed without therapy" (No-Alarm9339, 2024) is not misinforming on its face; it becomes misleading when the speaker implies, or readers infer, that therapy is unnecessary <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Hall, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Misleadingness may therefore arise not only from factual inaccuracies in a message but also from interactions between source or message properties and audience interpretation.
Yet a systematic account of these pathways in digital environments is still missing.

This gap matters because, amid declining institutional trust, platforms enable epistemic authority to emerge through visibility, relationships, and lived experience alongside professional credentials (Ienca et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This gap matters because, amid declining institutional trust, platforms enable epistemic authority to emerge through visibility, relationships, and lived experience alongside professional credentials <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Ienca et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Stigmatized, slow, or costly help-seeking may motivate audiences to interpret content as validating alternative treatments or explanations for distress (Choudhry et al., 2016; Kunda, 1990).
text.formatted: Stigmatized, slow, or costly help-seeking may motivate audiences to interpret content as validating alternative treatments or explanations for distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Choudhry et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Kunda, 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Mental health misleadingness warrants particular attention because vulnerability may be heightened among those most likely to seek such content: depressive symptoms have been associated with greater endorsement of health misinformation, possibly through negativity bias (Perlis et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Mental health misleadingness warrants particular attention because vulnerability may be heightened among those most likely to seek such content: depressive symptoms have been associated with greater endorsement of health misinformation, possibly through negativity bias <ref type="bibr">(Perlis et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Mental health misinformation refers to claims that are inadequately supported relative to the best available evidence (Bizzotto, De Bruijn, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Mental health misinformation refers to claims that are inadequately supported relative to the best available evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bizzotto, De Bruijn, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Misleading mental health content is a broader category of information disorder (Wardle & Derakhshan, 2017), encompassing false, unsupported, decontextualized, advanced under insufficient authority, or overgeneralized content that audiences may adopt as guidance for understanding, diagnosing, or treating psychological distress in ways that undermine clinical trust or care decisions.
text.formatted: Misleading mental health content is a broader category of information disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Wardle & Derakhshan, 2017)</ref>, encompassing false, unsupported, decontextualized, advanced under insufficient authority, or overgeneralized content that audiences may adopt as guidance for understanding, diagnosing, or treating psychological distress in ways that undermine clinical trust or care decisions.

text.text: Building on this definition, the proposed taxonomy has been developed through iterative conceptual synthesis (Jaakkola, 2020) and an interdisciplinary approach, building on insights from clinical psychology (e.g., Starvaggi et al., 2024), argumentation (e.g., Rubinelli & Diviani, 2025), health communication (e.g., Kaňková et al., 2025) and misinformation research (Vraga & Bode, 2020).
text.formatted: Building on this definition, the proposed taxonomy has been developed through iterative conceptual synthesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Jaakkola, 2020)</ref> and an interdisciplinary approach, building on insights from clinical psychology (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Starvaggi et al., 2024)</ref>, argumentation (e.g., Rubinelli & Diviani, 2025), health communication (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Kaňková et al., 2025)</ref> and misinformation research <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Vraga & Bode, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: I first reviewed literature on health and mental health misinformation and the popularization of clinical language, extracting mechanisms through which content has been described as misleading beyond factual inaccuracy.

I then organized these mechanisms according to a communication-process logic, distinguishing who advances a claim (source), what is communicated and how (message), and how it is received (decoding), following the distinction between encoding and decoding (Hall, 1980).
text.formatted: I then organized these mechanisms according to a communication-process logic, distinguishing who advances a claim (source), what is communicated and how (message), and how it is received (decoding), following the distinction between encoding and decoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Hall, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Categories were retained when they (a) fit the definition of misleading mental health content, (b) described a mechanism not reducible to another category, and (c) could be linked to a plausible pathway to harm in understanding, diagnosing, or treating psychological distress.
Categories were refined through discussion with scholars with expertise in mental health content online and misinformation.

Unlike existing health misinformation typologies, which classify content by topic, narrative, or degree of accuracy (e.g., Han et al., 2025; Yeung et al., 2022), this taxonomy adopts a communicative perspective: it locates misleadingness in three distinct but potentially cooccurring pathways: source-level, message-level, and decoding-levels (see Figure 1 and Table 1).
text.formatted: Unlike existing health misinformation typologies, which classify content by topic, narrative, or degree of accuracy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Han et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Yeung et al., 2022)</ref>, this taxonomy adopts a communicative perspective: it locates misleadingness in three distinct but potentially cooccurring pathways: source-level, message-level, and decoding-levels (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> and Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Source-level misleadingness concerns the epistemic positioning of the source advancing a specific claim.
In digital spaces, information is produced and shared not only through professional credentials but also through experiential expertise (i.e., lived experience; Bartsch et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In digital spaces, information is produced and shared not only through professional credentials but also through experiential expertise (i.e., lived experience; <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Bartsch et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This creates three related pathways to misleadingness, which differ in whether the source's authority has been misapplied, overextended, or entirely fabricated.

Authority mismatch occurs when a source communicates mental health content in a way that exceeds their credentials-for instance, when a non-clinician diagnoses another user with anxiety based on their social media narrative.
Lived-experience overreach occurs when a personal trajectory is presented as generalizable guidance for others.
This overreach can involve both optimistic and pessimistic accounts.

For example, "running cured my depression, so it can replace therapy for you too" may encourage treatment substitution, whereas "nothing has helped me, so treatment will not help you either" may foster the belief that treatment is ineffective.

Fabricated testimony occurs when credentials, identities or experiences are invented and/or synthetically produced to manufacture credibility (see phenomenon of astroturfing; Chan, 2024), as in deep-faked endorsements or AI-generated personas posing as healthcare professionals (Pinner, 2026).
text.formatted: Fabricated testimony occurs when credentials, identities or experiences are invented and/or synthetically produced to manufacture credibility (see phenomenon of astroturfing; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Chan, 2024)</ref>, as in deep-faked endorsements or AI-generated personas posing as healthcare professionals <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Pinner, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Message-level misleadingness concerns the epistemic, semantic, and rhetorical properties of the content itself.
It divides into epistemological distortion, lexical-semantic distortion, and rhetorical-representational distortion.

Epistemological distortion includes factual inaccuracy, where a claim directly contradicts available scientific evidence or clinical guidelines; unsupported claims, which lack adequate empirical support; evidence overclaiming, where preliminary evidence is presented as settled knowledge; and cherry-picking, where supportive findings are emphasized while contradicting evidence or contextual limitations are omitted.
This is the dimension on which most existing research on mental health misinformation has concentrated (Starvaggi et al., 2024; Swire-Thompson & Lazer, 2020).
text.formatted: This is the dimension on which most existing research on mental health misinformation has concentrated <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Starvaggi et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Swire-Thompson & Lazer, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Lexical-semantic distortions occur when the meaning or scope of a mental health concept is altered in ways that support inaccurate classification or inference, reflecting the diffusion of the "therapy speak" phenomenon on social media (i.e., the imprecise or superficial integration of psychotherapy language into everyday communication; Isern-Mas & Almagro, 2025).
text.formatted: Lexical-semantic distortions occur when the meaning or scope of a mental health concept is altered in ways that support inaccurate classification or inference, reflecting the diffusion of the "therapy speak" phenomenon on social media (i.e., the imprecise or superficial integration of psychotherapy language into everyday communication; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Isern-Mas & Almagro, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This includes concept creep, where clinical concepts expand to cover milder (vertical concept creep; e.g., depression, narcissism) or qualitatively different (horizontal concept creep; e.g., gaslighting, bipolar) behaviors (see Haslam, 2016).
text.formatted: This includes concept creep, where clinical concepts expand to cover milder (vertical concept creep; e.g., depression, narcissism) or qualitatively different (horizontal concept creep; e.g., gaslighting, bipolar) behaviors (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Haslam, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Rhetorical-representational distortion concerns how mental health experiences are presented.

In spiritual bypassing, spiritual language is used to dismiss unresolved psychological distress (Welwood, 2000); symptom trivialization minimizes clinically relevant symptoms; glamorization romanticizes psychological distress, presenting it as desirable or identityenhancing (Blackburn & Hogg, 2024); and stigmatizing representation attaches false assumptions to people with mental health conditions.
text.formatted: In spiritual bypassing, spiritual language is used to dismiss unresolved psychological distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Welwood, 2000)</ref>; symptom trivialization minimizes clinically relevant symptoms; glamorization romanticizes psychological distress, presenting it as desirable or identityenhancing <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blackburn & Hogg, 2024)</ref>; and stigmatizing representation attaches false assumptions to people with mental health conditions.

text.text: Decoding-level misleadingness arises through the interaction between source or message properties and audiences' interpretive processes.
The source may share a personal experience or subjective opinion; the problem appears only once audiences use it as guidance for diagnosis or treatment.

These processes may be shaped by mental health literacy, prior treatment experiences, and motivated reasoning (Kunda, 1990). Hall's (1980) encoding/decoding framework is useful here: a message encoded as a personal story can be decoded as clinical guidance.
text.formatted: These processes may be shaped by mental health literacy, prior treatment experiences, and motivated reasoning <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Kunda, 1990</ref>). <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Hall's (1980)</ref> encoding/decoding framework is useful here: a message encoded as a personal story can be decoded as clinical guidance.

text.text: Opinion-to-guidance uptake occurs when a personal opinion is interpreted as general advice, for example when negative opinions or experiences concerning therapy are interpreted as general evidence against professional care (Bizzotto, Schulz, et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Opinion-to-guidance uptake occurs when a personal opinion is interpreted as general advice, for example when negative opinions or experiences concerning therapy are interpreted as general evidence against professional care <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bizzotto, Schulz, et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Treatment/dosage comparison occurs when medication names, dosages, or recovery timelines disclosed by others are used as benchmarks for evaluating and self-managing one's care.

Symptom-to-diagnosis inference occurs when a viewer interprets a symptom, for instance discussed by a mental health content creator, as evidence of having the associated disorder because they recognize that symptom in themselves.

text.text: Misleading mental health content present online cannot be understood only as the circulation of inaccurate claims: This article argues that mental health content may also become misleading through mismatches with epistemic authority, evidentiality, conceptual distortion, and how audiences interpret content.
Although the examples provided are text-based, the taxonomy is modality-agnostic.

The taxonomy broadens the study of mental health online content beyond assessments of factual accuracy, conceptualizing misleadingness as a multidimensional phenomenon that may arise from the relationship among a claim, the epistemic authority supporting it, its evidentiary and representational organization, and the inferences audiences derive from it.
This perspective creates a basis for developing measures that capture pathways to misleadingness that conventional accuracy-based classifications may overlook.
Further research should test whether the proposed pathways produce distinct cognitive, affective, and behavioral outcomes.
Finally, research should examine how platform environments shape the production, visibility, and uptake of different forms of misleading content.
Platform affordances, such as popularity metrics, credential displays, and algorithmic recommendation, may influence how epistemic authority is attributed (Bartsch et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Platform affordances, such as popularity metrics, credential displays, and algorithmic recommendation, may influence how epistemic authority is attributed <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bartsch et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: For clinicians, the taxonomy provides a vocabulary for assessing how patients might interpret the mental health content encountered online.
For educators, it can anchor media literacy interventions that address source-checking in addition to fact-checking.
For platforms and policymakers, it suggests that flagging or moderation limited to false claims may overlook misleading content arising through other pathways.
This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed.
